title: The Winter's Tale
author: William Shakespeare
setting: The court of Sicilia and, sixteen years later, a sheep-shearing feast on the coast of Bohemia
lengthNote: Around 3,000 lines, with a sixteen-year gap opened in the middle of them
openingLine: If you shall chance, Camillo, to visit Bohemia, on the like occasion whereon my services are now on foot
summary: A king watches his wife be courteous to his oldest friend and decides, in the space of nine lines, that she has betrayed him. Three acts later a bear has eaten a nobleman, a baby has been left on a beach and sixteen years have gone past in a speech. What returns is not the world he broke but a second one built beside it, and the play's last scene asks an audience to believe a thing it has been told twice is impossible.

sourceText.label: Globe/Moby text of The Winter's Tale
sourceText.note: Line numbers follow the traditional Globe numbering. The only early text is the First Folio, generally thought to have been set from a scribal transcript.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: One of the late plays, close in date to Cymbeline and The Tempest.

atAGlance.label: First seen
atAGlance.note: Simon Forman recorded a performance at the Globe and wrote down what he took from it — chiefly a warning about trusting confidence men.

atAGlance.label: Chief source
atAGlance.note: Robert Greene's prose romance of 1588, whose jealous king dies at the end. Shakespeare keeps the plot and refuses the ending.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: Three acts of tragedy, a speech from Time, and two acts of pastoral comedy that have to carry the first three.

structure.label: Act I
structure.title: Nine lines, and a marriage destroyed
structure.summary: Polixenes has been visiting for nine months and means to leave; Hermione persuades him to stay because her husband asked her to. Watching them talk, Leontes decides they are lovers, and there is no Iago, no handkerchief and no evidence of any kind. By the end of the act he has ordered his most trusted counsellor to poison a king.

scenes.title: Two courtiers
scenes.summary: Camillo and Archidamus praise the friendship of the kings and the promise of the young prince.

scenes.title: Too hot, too hot
scenes.summary: Hermione wins the argument her husband could not, and Leontes watches her hand in another man's and goes mad in public.

structure.label: Act II
structure.title: A queen arrested and an oracle sent for
structure.summary: Hermione is taken from her son in the middle of a ghost story and imprisoned; she gives birth in the cell. Paulina carries the baby to the king expecting the sight of it to work, and is called a witch for her trouble. Leontes has already sent to Delphos, and announces that he will believe the god whatever the god says.

scenes.title: The sad tale
scenes.summary: Mamillius begins a winter's tale and is interrupted by his father's guards; Hermione is charged and taken away.

scenes.title: The prison
scenes.summary: Paulina learns of the birth and decides to carry the child to its father herself.

scenes.title: The infant refused
scenes.summary: Paulina lays the baby at the king's feet and argues; Antigonus is sworn to carry it to a desert place and leave it.

structure.label: Act III
structure.title: The oracle, the deaths, and the bear
structure.summary: Hermione defends herself in the clearest speech in the play, the oracle clears her in five clauses, and Leontes rejects it out loud. His son dies within a minute of the blasphemy and his wife within two. Then the play changes countries, a storm sinks a ship, a bear takes Antigonus, and a shepherd finds a baby and says the first kind thing anyone has said for three acts.

scenes.title: Returning from Delphos
scenes.summary: Cleomenes and Dion describe the sweet air and the deafening voice of the oracle, and hope for a good outcome.

scenes.title: The trial
scenes.summary: Hermione speaks for her honour, the oracle is read, Leontes denies it, and Mamillius and Hermione are both reported dead.

scenes.title: Things dying, things newborn
scenes.summary: Antigonus leaves the baby on the Bohemian coast and exits pursued by a bear; a shepherd and his son find the child and the wreck.

structure.label: Act IV
structure.title: Sixteen years, a sheep-shearing and a pedlar
structure.summary: Time appears as a chorus, turns the glass and moves the play on. In Bohemia the foundling is a shepherd's daughter presiding over a feast, a prince is courting her under a false name, and a thief with a ballad-sheet is working the crowd. Then Polixenes tears off his disguise and threatens everyone, and the young couple run for Sicilia with the help of the man who fled it.

scenes.title: Time
scenes.summary: The chorus turns his hourglass, apologises for the leap and sets the second half in motion.

scenes.title: Camillo asks to go home
scenes.summary: Polixenes refuses, and they agree to go in disguise to the shepherd's cottage where the prince keeps disappearing.

scenes.title: Autolycus
scenes.summary: A pedlar and former courtier sings on the road, picks the Clown's pocket by pretending to be robbed, and goes to the feast.

scenes.title: The sheep-shearing
scenes.summary: Perdita gives out flowers and argues about art and nature with a disguised king who then forbids the match and threatens her with death.

structure.label: Act V
structure.title: Recognitions, and a chapel
structure.summary: Leontes has spent sixteen years doing penance under Paulina's supervision. The lovers arrive, the pursuing king arrives, the tokens are produced and the reunion of father and daughter is deliberately kept offstage and reported by gentlemen. The play saves its one visible wonder for last, in a chapel, with a curtain and a piece of music.

scenes.title: Penitence
scenes.summary: Leontes is urged to remarry and Paulina forbids it; Florizel and Perdita arrive claiming a diplomatic errand.

scenes.title: The reunion, reported
scenes.summary: Three gentlemen describe the discovery of Perdita's identity to one another, and the Clown becomes a gentleman born.

scenes.title: The statue
scenes.summary: Paulina draws a curtain on a figure of Hermione aged sixteen years, requires the onlookers to awake their faith, and calls for music.

characters.name: Leontes
characters.summary: His jealousy has no source outside himself, and the play makes that a formal problem: the verse breaks apart into half-lines, parentheses and obscene punning within seconds of the first suspicion. He is given the longest penance in Shakespeare and the play never quite says it has been enough.
characters.clue: He needs no villain to persuade him, convicts a queen on the evidence of a handshake, and spends sixteen years visiting a grave at the instruction of the woman who chose it.

characters.name: Hermione
characters.summary: She is witty and entirely at ease in the first scene, which is what condemns her, and at the trial she argues from honour rather than innocence because innocence has already been ruled inadmissible. She has perhaps eighty lines after the trial and none at all to her husband in the final scene.
characters.clue: She wins an argument on her husband's behalf and is charged with adultery for it; sixteen years later she is a statue with wrinkles.

characters.name: Paulina
characters.role: A lady of the Sicilian court, Antigonus's wife
characters.summary: She says the unsayable to a king in Act III and then organises the next sixteen years of his life. Whether she hid a living woman for that long or performed a miracle is left deliberately unresolved, and she loses a husband to a bear and is handed a new one in the last thirty lines.
characters.clue: She calls a king a tyrant to his face, keeps something behind a curtain for sixteen years, and tells a court that it is required to awake its faith.

characters.name: Perdita
characters.role: Leontes and Hermione's lost daughter, raised as a shepherd's child
characters.summary: She presides over the sheep-shearing in borrowed finery and is uncomfortable in it, and she holds her own in an argument about grafting against a king. The play is careful that her authority looks natural without ever settling whether that is breeding, upbringing or the pastoral convention doing its work.
characters.clue: She is dressed as a goddess for a feast she thinks is above her, refuses to grow streaked flowers, and wants spring flowers for a living lover rather than a corpse.

characters.name: Polixenes
characters.summary: He begins as the innocent party and ends the fourth act threatening to have a shepherd's daughter's face scratched with briars. The play gives him the elegant argument that art is itself a part of nature, and then has him forbid exactly the kind of grafting he has just defended.
characters.clue: He argues that crossing a noble bud with a baser stock is nature's own art, and forty lines later threatens death to anyone who lets his son marry a shepherdess.

characters.name: Camillo
characters.role: A Sicilian lord, later Polixenes's counsellor
characters.summary: Ordered to commit a murder, he warns the victim and leaves with him, which is the one action in the first half that prevents a death. He then spends sixteen years homesick and engineers the escape to Sicilia largely because he wants to see the place again.
characters.clue: Told to poison a king, he takes him abroad instead, and later sends a prince and a shepherdess to the country he is longing for.

characters.name: Florizel
characters.role: Prince of Bohemia, courting as Doricles
characters.summary: He is in the same disguise Rosalind and Viola wear, and he uses it only to be poorer than he is. His praise of Perdita dancing is the most beautiful speech in the play and also, read carefully, a wish that she would never do anything else.
characters.clue: He courts under a false name in shepherd's clothes and tells his love he wishes she could dance for ever, which is a compliment with a door in it.
traits: readier to lose a kingdom than to argue for one

characters.name: Autolycus
characters.summary: He arrives after the interval of sixteen years and changes the play's weather entirely, singing, cheating and selling printed ballads about impossible events to people who buy them because they are printed. He is the only character who profits from the happy ending without contributing anything to it.
characters.clue: Named after the son of Mercury, littered under the same planet, he picks a pocket by pretending to have been robbed and sells ballads of fish and usurers' wives.

characters.name: Mamillius
characters.summary: He is beginning a ghost story for his mother — a sad tale, because it is winter — when the guards come in, and the play takes its title from the tale he never finishes. He dies of what a servant calls mere conceit and fear, and nothing in the last act replaces him.
characters.clue: He is told a sad tale is best for winter, gets two lines into one, and is the reason the ending cannot be called a restoration.

characters.name: Antigonus
characters.summary: He argues for the queen, is bullied into swearing an oath, and then keeps it — which is the play's clearest illustration of how obedience does the damage that tyranny orders. His death is the most famous stage direction in the language, and his last line is one of the quietest.
characters.clue: He carries a baby to a beach because he swore he would, says he is gone for ever, and is right.

themes.name: Jealousy without a cause
themes.summary: Shakespeare had already written the version with a tempter; here he removes him. Leontes supplies his own evidence, his own interpretation and his own verdict inside a single speech, and the play shows the process in the grammar — clauses that start over, brackets inside brackets, words that turn obscene as he handles them.
themes.development: It arrives fully formed in 1.2, hardens into law in 2.1 and 2.3, and survives even the oracle in 3.2 until a child's death breaks it in a single line.

themes.name: Time and what it cannot mend
themes.summary: The play's hinge is a chorus who turns an hourglass and moves the action on sixteen years, and everything after that is about what can and cannot be recovered. The daughter comes back and the wife comes back; the son does not, and neither does Antigonus.
themes.development: A boy's unfinished tale in 2.1, the leap of Act IV, and in 5.3 a statue deliberately carved with sixteen years of age on it so that the time cannot be pretended away.

themes.name: Art and nature
themes.summary: The argument is conducted explicitly over grafted flowers in 4.4 and then acted out in the last scene, where a woman is presented as a painted stone. Perdita will not have improved carnations; Paulina asks a court to accept a work of art that breathes.
themes.development: Polixenes argues that the art itself is nature and immediately contradicts himself in practice; the statue scene answers him by refusing to say which it is.

themes.name: Faith, oracles and wonder
themes.summary: An oracle is read out, believed by everyone except the one man who sent for it, and vindicated by a death within the minute. In the last scene nothing supernatural is claimed and everything depends on whether the onlookers will do what Paulina asks and awake their faith.
themes.development: Apollo in Act III speaks and is denied; in Act V there is no god at all, only music, a curtain and an instruction.

themes.name: The women who hold the line
themes.summary: Hermione argues for her honour in a court that has already convicted her; Paulina tells a king he is a tyrant and then runs his conscience for sixteen years; Perdita refuses a king's argument about breeding to his face. The men in this play give orders and the women decide what will actually happen.
themes.development: Hermione's defence in 3.2, Paulina's denunciation a hundred lines later, and in 5.3 a woman directing every other character on stage, including two kings.

themes.name: Court and country, tragedy and comedy
themes.summary: The play is built in two unequal halves and refuses to blend them: a claustrophobic court where a man watches his wife's hands, and an open field with a pedlar, a dance and a cheat. The famous impossible bear stands exactly between them.
themes.development: Three acts of tragedy, an exit pursued by a bear, and a shepherd's remark about things dying and things newborn — which is the play describing its own form.

techniques.name: Broken syntax
techniques.definition: Sentences that fracture, restart or bury themselves in parenthesis to show a mind under strain.
techniques.inThisBook: Leontes's speeches in 1.2 and 2.1 are among the hardest passages Shakespeare wrote, and the difficulty is the point: the audience has to work out the thought at the same speed he is failing to.

techniques.name: The Chorus
techniques.definition: A figure outside the action who addresses the audience and moves it through time or space.
techniques.inThisBook: Time appears at the start of Act IV to turn his glass and skip sixteen years, apologising for the liberty — a device Sidney had mocked in print, used here without embarrassment.

techniques.name: The reported scene
techniques.definition: A major event described by witnesses rather than performed.
techniques.inThisBook: The reunion of Leontes and Perdita — the scene any other play would build to — is handed to three gentlemen in 5.2, so that the statue can be the only wonder the audience actually sees.

techniques.name: Festival and song
techniques.definition: A set-piece of country celebration, with dance, ballads and the giving of flowers.
techniques.inThisBook: The sheep-shearing in 4.4 is the longest scene in Shakespeare, and it is built of ballads, a pedlar's pack and a flower speech that turns into a lament halfway through.

techniques.name: The sustained stage image
techniques.definition: A piece of staging held long enough to become the play's argument.
techniques.inThisBook: A woman standing motionless behind a curtain for eighty lines while a court talks about her: the last scene works because nobody is allowed to touch her until she moves.

techniques.name: Tragicomic structure
techniques.definition: A play that goes as far as tragedy will take it and then turns.
techniques.inThisBook: Two deaths and an abandonment in Act III are followed by a stage direction about a bear and a scene of comic misunderstanding; the join is left visible on purpose.

quotations.text: Too hot, too hot! To mingle friendship far is mingling bloods. I have tremor cordis on me: my heart dances; But not for joy; not joy.
quotations.speaker: Leontes
quotations.context: An aside, the instant Hermione succeeds in persuading Polixenes to stay.
quotations.analysis: This is the whole onset of the jealousy, and it occupies four lines. 'Tremor cordis' is a physician's term, so he reaches for a diagnosis before he reaches for an accusation; the repetitions — too hot, mingle and mingling, not for joy, not joy — are a man arguing with something already decided.

quotations.text: But to be paddling palms and pinching fingers, As now they are, and making practised smiles, As in a looking-glass, and then to sigh, as 'twere The mort o' the deer
quotations.speaker: Leontes
quotations.context: Continuing the aside, describing what he can see across the stage.
quotations.analysis: Everything he lists is something the audience can watch happening, which is what makes the scene so uncomfortable to stage: a director must decide how much of this is true. The hunting horn blown at a deer's death was a stock image for the sigh after sex, so the innuendo is doing the work that evidence cannot.

quotations.text: A sad tale's best for winter: I have one Of sprites and goblins.
quotations.speaker: Mamillius
quotations.context: Beginning a story for his mother and her ladies, moments before the guards arrive.
quotations.analysis: The play takes its title from a child's game and then interrupts it for good: he gets two lines further before his father walks in. Placing the phrase here rather than in the happy fifth act makes the title a description of Acts I to III, not of the ending.

quotations.text: There may be in the cup A spider steep'd, and one may drink, depart, And yet partake no venom, for his knowledge Is not infected: but if one present The abhorr'd ingredient to his eye, make known How he hath drunk, he cracks his gorge, his sides, With violent hefts.
quotations.speaker: Leontes
quotations.context: On being told that Polixenes and Camillo have fled by ship.
quotations.analysis: It is a brilliant image and it proves nothing whatever: the argument is that knowing makes the poison work, which conveniently means his own conviction is itself the evidence. He ends the sentence with 'I have drunk, and seen the spider', having drunk nothing and seen only two men leaving in a hurry.

quotations.text: You speak a language that I understand not: My life stands in the level of your dreams, Which I'll lay down.
quotations.speaker: Hermione
quotations.context: At her trial, answering the charge of conspiracy.
quotations.analysis: 'In the level of' is an archery term — she is standing in the line of his aim — and the aim is a dream. Leontes answers by taking the word off her: 'Your actions are my dreams', which is the play's most compact statement of how a delusion defends itself.

quotations.text: if powers divine Behold our human actions, as they do, I doubt not then but innocence shall make False accusation blush and tyranny Tremble at patience.
quotations.speaker: Hermione
quotations.context: The opening of her defence, before the court.
quotations.analysis: She makes blushing and trembling the business of the accusers rather than the accused, which reverses the whole physical vocabulary of a trial. The conditional at the start — 'if powers divine behold' — is the risk she is taking, and within a hundred lines Apollo answers it, and Leontes refuses the answer.

quotations.text: Hermione is chaste; Polixenes blameless; Camillo a true subject; Leontes a jealous tyrant; his innocent babe truly begotten; and the king shall live without an heir, if that which is lost be not found.
quotations.speaker: An Officer
quotations.context: Reading the sealed oracle aloud in the courtroom.
quotations.analysis: Five flat verdicts and then one condition, and the condition is the plot of the last two acts. Everything before the final clause is in the present tense and settled; the play's whole second half hangs on the word 'if', which is the only uncertainty Apollo allows.

quotations.text: Apollo's angry; and the heavens themselves Do strike at my injustice.
quotations.speaker: Leontes
quotations.context: One line after a servant reports that his son is dead.
quotations.analysis: The delusion that survived a god's direct testimony collapses the moment a child dies, which is a brutal piece of arithmetic on the play's part. Note that he still makes the news about himself — the heavens are striking at his injustice, not at Mamillius.

quotations.text: What studied torments, tyrant, hast for me? What wheels? racks? fires? what flaying? boiling? In leads or oils? what old or newer torture Must I receive, whose every word deserves To taste of thy most worst?
quotations.speaker: Paulina
quotations.context: Returning to the court with the news that the queen is dead.
quotations.analysis: She lists the punishments before she delivers the news, which is a way of making it impossible to silence her: every torment has already been named and accepted. The word 'tyrant' is placed inside the first question, where a king's title would go.

quotations.text: The day frowns more and more: thou'rt like to have A lullaby too rough: I never saw The heavens so dim by day. A savage clamour! Well may I get aboard! This is the chase: I am gone for ever.
quotations.speaker: Antigonus
quotations.context: On the Bohemian coast, having just laid the baby down; the next line of the text is the stage direction.
quotations.analysis: 'A lullaby too rough' is addressed to an infant he is abandoning in a storm, and it is the gentlest thing said in three acts. The last four words are both a cry of terror and a piece of plain information, and the stage direction that follows them is the most famous in the language.

quotations.text: Heavy matters! heavy matters! but look thee here, boy. Now bless thyself: thou mettest with things dying, I with things newborn.
quotations.speaker: Shepherd
quotations.context: To his son, who has just described the shipwreck and the bear, while holding the baby he has found.
quotations.analysis: The play's structure is stated out loud by a man who has no idea he is describing it: one half of the stage has a wreck on it and the other half a child. It is also the only line in Shakespeare that could serve as a definition of tragicomedy, and it is given to a shepherd in prose.

quotations.text: My father named me Autolycus; who being, as I am, littered under Mercury, was likewise a snapper-up of unconsidered trifles.
quotations.speaker: Autolycus
quotations.context: Introducing himself to the audience on the road to the sheep-shearing.
quotations.analysis: Mercury was the god of thieves and of eloquence, and Autolycus in Homer was his son; the name is a joke for anyone who has it and a good name for a pedlar for anyone who has not. 'Littered' is a word for animals, and he applies it to himself without complaint.

quotations.text: You see, sweet maid, we marry A gentler scion to the wildest stock, And make conceive a bark of baser kind By bud of nobler race: this is an art Which does mend nature, change it rather, but The art itself is nature.
quotations.speaker: Polixenes
quotations.context: Disguised at the sheep-shearing, arguing with Perdita about grafted flowers.
quotations.analysis: The argument is that human art is one of nature's own methods, and it is unanswerable — Perdita simply says 'So it is' and then refuses to do it anyway. The joke is savage: within forty lines the same speaker will forbid his noble son to marry a baser stock and threaten the girl with death.

quotations.text: O Proserpina, For the flowers now, that frighted thou let'st fall From Dis's waggon! daffodils, That come before the swallow dares, and take The winds of March with beauty
quotations.speaker: Perdita
quotations.context: Wishing she had spring flowers to give the young women at the feast.
quotations.analysis: Every flower in the speech is one she does not have, so the loveliest passage in the play is a list of absences. Proserpina was also a daughter stolen from her mother and returned for half the year — Perdita invokes her own story without knowing it, which is the closest the play comes to telling her who she is.

quotations.text: when you do dance, I wish you A wave o' the sea, that you might ever do Nothing but that; move still, still so, And own no other function
quotations.speaker: Florizel
quotations.context: Praising Perdita as she moves among the guests.
quotations.analysis: 'Move still, still so' means keep moving and keep still at once, which is what a wave does and what a statue cannot — the play will collect on that image in the last scene. The wish is also faintly alarming: he would like her to do nothing else ever, and the speech turns her actions into a series of held poses.

quotations.text: No more such wives; therefore, no wife: one worse, And better used, would make her sainted spirit Again possess her corpse, and on this stage, Where we're offenders now, appear soul-vex'd, And begin, 'Why to me?'
quotations.speaker: Leontes
quotations.context: Refusing, in front of Paulina, the court's suggestion that he remarry.
quotations.analysis: He imagines his dead wife returning to reproach him, in a theatre, on a stage — and two scenes later she does return, without reproaching him at all. 'Where we're offenders now' turns the court into a playhouse and the living into the guilty party, which is exactly the arrangement of the final scene.

quotations.text: Chide me, dear stone, that I may say indeed Thou art Hermione; or rather, thou art she In thy not chiding, for she was as tender As infancy and grace.
quotations.speaker: Leontes
quotations.context: The first words spoken after Paulina draws the curtain.
quotations.analysis: He asks the statue to scold him and then decides its silence is more like her, which lets him have the rebuke and the forgiveness at once. Everything he says in this scene is addressed to an object, and the audience has been given no more information than he has.

quotations.text: So much the more our carver's excellence; Which lets go by some sixteen years and makes her As she lived now.
quotations.speaker: Paulina
quotations.context: Explaining why the statue looks older than the queen Leontes remembers.
quotations.analysis: The wrinkles are the play's proof that the reconciliation is not a reversal: the sixteen years are carved into the object everyone is looking at. It is also a very good lie, and the audience is invited to notice that a sculptor who aged his subject would be doing something no sculptor does.

quotations.text: It is required You do awake your faith. Then all stand still; On: those that think it is unlawful business I am about, let them depart.
quotations.speaker: Paulina
quotations.context: Before calling for music and telling the statue to descend.
quotations.analysis: The instruction is given to the people on stage and, unavoidably, to the people watching them: a theatre audience is always being asked to do this, and here the request is made out loud. 'Required' is the hardest word in the sentence — not invited, not encouraged, and with an exit offered to anyone who will not.

quotations.text: O, she's warm! If this be magic, let it be an art Lawful as eating.
quotations.speaker: Leontes
quotations.context: Taking Hermione's hand as she steps down from the pedestal.
quotations.analysis: Three words settle a question the whole scene has hung on, and they are about temperature rather than identity. The comparison he reaches for is eating — the most ordinary bodily fact available — which quietly refuses the supernatural reading while leaving it standing.

quotations.text: That she is living, Were it but told you, should be hooted at Like an old tale: but it appears she lives, Though yet she speak not.
quotations.speaker: Paulina
quotations.context: As Hermione embraces Leontes and the others ask where she has been.
quotations.analysis: The play calls its own plot ridiculous for the third time, and the defence is that this one is being seen rather than reported. It is also an exact description of what the audience is doing: accepting on stage what it would hoot at in a story, which is the difference the last act is built to demonstrate.

quotations.text: You gods, look down And from your sacred vials pour your graces Upon my daughter's head!
quotations.speaker: Hermione
quotations.context: Her first words after sixteen years, spoken once Paulina has turned her towards Perdita.
quotations.analysis: She speaks to the gods, then to her daughter, and never once to her husband — the reunion the play has been building towards turns out to be with the child. Her only explanation is that she preserved herself because the oracle gave hope the baby was alive, which makes the marriage a piece of unfinished business the play leaves alone.

timeline.label: Robert Greene's Pandosto published
timeline.detail: The prose romance Shakespeare follows closely, and whose jealous king kills himself at the end.

timeline.label: Greene dies, having attacked Shakespeare in print
timeline.detail: The pamphlet that calls him an upstart crow appeared in the same year; twenty years later Shakespeare took Greene's plot.

timeline.label: The Winter's Tale most likely written
timeline.detail: Usually dated 1609–11, among the late plays and close to Cymbeline and The Tempest.

timeline.label: Simon Forman sees the play at the Globe
timeline.detail: His notebook entry of 15 May records the plot, the bear and, at length, Autolycus; the moral he draws is to beware of trusting feigned beggars.

timeline.label: Played at court for Princess Elizabeth's wedding festivities
timeline.detail: The King's Men gave a long series of plays for the marriage of James's daughter, and this was among them.

timeline.label: Jonson mocks plays of this kind in Bartholomew Fair
timeline.detail: The induction to Bartholomew Fair jeers at plays full of servant-monsters and drolleries — a contemporary judgement on exactly this kind of writing.

timeline.label: First Folio
timeline.detail: The only early text, printed last among the comedies and generally thought to have been set from a scribe's transcript.

timeline.label: Garrick's Florizel and Perdita
timeline.detail: An adaptation that kept the pastoral and cut most of the first three acts, and held the stage for decades.

timeline.label: The full play returns to the London stage
timeline.detail: The nineteenth century restored the tragic first half, and the statue scene became one of the great set pieces of the English theatre.

places.name: Sicily
places.note: Leontes's court, the trial, and the chapel in Paulina's house.

places.name: Bohemia
places.note: Polixenes's kingdom and the sheep-shearing — given a sea-coast by the play, which Bohemia has never had.

places.name: Delphi
places.note: The play calls it Delphos and makes it an island; Cleomenes and Dion sail there for the oracle.

places.name: Delos
places.note: The Aegean island sacred to Apollo, routinely confused with Delphi in Shakespeare's day and the reason the ambassadors go by sea.

places.name: The Globe, Bankside
places.note: Where Simon Forman saw the play in May 1611 and wrote down what he made of it.

criticalViews.position: A play about repentance and grace
criticalViews.summary: The oldest reading takes the last scene at its word: sixteen years of penance are answered by something that looks like resurrection, and the language of faith, awakening and redemption is the play's own.
criticalViews.counter: Mamillius and Antigonus stay dead, and the play makes a point of the wrinkles — nothing is given back unaltered.

criticalViews.summary: The chorus, the reported reunion, the curtain and the instruction to awake your faith all point at the playhouse: what the last act asks of Leontes is exactly what a performance asks of an audience.
criticalViews.counter: It can make the reconciliation feel like a trick, when the text gives Hermione a plain and unmagical explanation of where she has been.

criticalViews.position: Where was Hermione for sixteen years?
criticalViews.summary: The text supports two readings — a concealment managed by Paulina, or a genuine restoration — and criticism has long argued about which the staging should imply, since the answer changes what kind of play this is.
criticalViews.counter: The scene is written so that neither reading can be ruled out, which suggests the ambiguity is the effect rather than an oversight.

criticalViews.summary: Feminist criticism has noted how completely the second half depends on women — Paulina's management, Perdita's authority, Hermione's silence — and how little the restored marriage is allowed to say for itself.
criticalViews.counter: The same reading has to account for Paulina being handed a new husband in the last thirty lines, with no line of her own to answer it.

essayQuestions.question: How does Shakespeare present Leontes's jealousy, and what is the effect of giving it no cause?
essayQuestions.focus: Language, evidence and the absence of an Iago
plan: Compare the opening with Othello: there is no tempter here, and the suspicion takes nine lines.
Analyse the syntax of 1.2.134 onward — the restarts, the parentheses, the sexual punning that arrives before the accusation.
Use the spider speech at 2.1.51 to show the jealousy generating its own proof.
Examine 3.2: the oracle is denied, and only a child's death breaks the delusion.
Conclude on what the missing motive does to an audience, which is left with nothing to blame but a mind.

essayQuestions.question: Discuss the function of the play's two halves.
plan: Set out the shape: three acts of tragedy, a chorus, two acts of pastoral comedy.
Read 3.3 closely — the abandonment, the bear, the Clown's comic account of a drowning — as the point where the genres change hands.
Use the Shepherd's 'things dying, I with things newborn' as the play's own description of its form.
Show how the second half keeps the first in view: sixteen years, an aged statue, a dead son never replaced.
Argue whether the join is a flaw the play survives or the whole point of it.

essayQuestions.question: What is Paulina for?
plan: Begin with 2.2 and 2.3, where she decides on her own initiative to confront a king with his daughter.
Analyse the denunciation at 3.2.192 and note that she lists the tortures before delivering the news.
Trace her control of the sixteen years: the daily visits to the grave, the veto on remarriage in 5.1.
Read 5.3 as a piece of direction — the curtain, the standstill, the music, the instruction about faith.
Weigh the ending, in which the play's most independent character is given a husband in a single line.

essayQuestions.question: 'The last scene works because the audience is asked to do something.' Discuss.
essayQuestions.focus: Faith, wonder and the reported reunion
plan: Note first what the play declines to show: the recognition of Perdita is handed to three gentlemen in 5.2.
Establish what the audience knows and does not know going into 5.3, and what a production can choose to signal.
Analyse 'It is required You do awake your faith' as an instruction aimed past the stage.
Consider 'O, she's warm' and the comparison to eating — the wonder is confirmed by the most ordinary evidence available.
Decide what Hermione's silence towards her husband does to the effect, and whether the scene is a reward or a question.

discussionQuestions: Leontes becomes jealous in nine lines with no evidence at all. Is that harder or easier to watch than Othello's slow poisoning?
The reunion of father and daughter happens offstage and is described by strangers. Why give away the scene most plays would build to?
Was Hermione alive for sixteen years, or restored? Does a production have to decide?
Mamillius never comes back, and nobody in the last scene mentions him. What does that silence do to the ending?
Bohemia has no sea-coast, and the play knows it. Does the impossibility matter, or is it part of the invitation?

related.why: The other late play built on loss, a long interval and a reconciliation the text will not quite guarantee.
Written within a year or two, with the same machinery: a wronged wife, a lost child, an oracle and a recognition scene.
The same disease with a cause supplied, which makes the comparison the fastest way to see what this play is doing.
The first of the late romances, with a chorus, a sea and a daughter restored to a father who has stopped speaking.
The earlier pastoral, where the country festival is the whole play rather than the cure for the first half of one.
